prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Apollo 13 was launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on 11 April 1970, the third mission planned to land men on the Moon. The commander was Jim Lovell, on his fourth spaceflight, and the lunar module pilot was Fred Haise, who was making his first. The command module pilot was Jack Swigert, who joined the crew only two days before launch. Ken Mattingly had been due to fly, but Charlie Duke, a colleague who had been working with the crew, developed German measles, and Mattingly had no immunity to it. The flight surgeons removed him, and Swigert, the backup, took his place. The spacecraft consisted of the command module Odyssey, the service module behind it, and the lunar module Aquarius, which was to land at a highland site called Fra Mauro.

The first two days went smoothly. The crew made a small course correction, held a television broadcast from the spacecraft, and settled into their routine. On 13 April, about 56 hours into the flight and some 330,000 kilometres from Earth, mission control asked Swigert to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module. This was routine, and it kept the supercold contents from stratifying. Shortly afterwards the crew heard a bang and felt a shudder, and a warning showed a drop in electrical power. Swigert reported that they had had a problem, and Lovell repeated it for the ground. Lovell looked out of a window and saw gas venting into space from the side of the service module.

The cause lay in oxygen tank number two. The tank had been dropped a short distance during handling in 1968, and this probably damaged its internal fill tube. Later, during a ground test before the launch, the heaters inside the tank ran far longer than intended. The thermostat switches that should have shut them off had been rated for 28 volts, while the ground power supply delivered 65, and the switches fused shut. The heaters burned away much of the Teflon insulation on the wiring inside the tank. When Swigert switched on the stirring fans, a spark in the bare wiring ignited the oxygen. The pressure rose until the tank failed and blew a panel off the side of the service module. The blast also damaged the second oxygen tank, which began to leak.

The service module's fuel cells needed oxygen to make electricity and drinking water, and within about three hours both tanks were empty. The command module had only its own batteries and a small reserve of oxygen, which it needed for the return to Earth. The flight director, Gene Kranz, and his team in Houston decided that the crew should use the lunar module as a lifeboat. Aquarius was built to support two men for about two days on the lunar surface, and it now had to keep three alive for roughly four. The crew moved into it and shut down nearly everything in Odyssey, so that its batteries would last for re-entry.

The spacecraft was on a path that would take it around the Moon and out into space, and it would not return to Earth unaided. Earlier in the flight it had been moved off a so-called free-return trajectory to allow for the landing at Fra Mauro, so the first task was to bring it back toward Earth. About five hours after the explosion the crew used the lunar module's descent engine for a short burn to restore the free return. They then passed behind the Moon, at about 250 kilometres above its surface, and reached a greater distance from Earth than any humans before or since, 400,171 kilometres. After they rounded the Moon, a second burn with the descent engine, lasting about four and a half minutes, sped up the return and brought the landing forward by around ten hours. It also moved the splashdown to the Pacific, where the recovery ships were waiting.

The remaining problems were ones of supply. To save electricity, the crew switched off most of the lunar module's systems, including the heaters, and the cabin temperature fell to about 6 degrees Celsius. Water was rationed to a few ounces per man each day, because it was needed to cool the electronics. Lovell lost about 14 pounds in weight over the flight. Haise developed a fever and a urinary infection, and he spent much of the return unwell. Sleep was difficult in the cold, and the men took turns resting in the command module, which was colder still.

The most serious difficulty was carbon dioxide. The lithium hydroxide canisters that removed it from the air were limited in number in the lunar module, and the spare canisters in the command module were square, while the lunar module's system used round ones. As the gas level rose toward a dangerous point, engineers on the ground assembled a device from items known to be on board, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual cover, suit hoses and duct tape. They read the instructions to the crew over the radio, and the crew built the adaptor and fitted a square canister to a round socket. The gas level fell, and it stayed within safe limits to the end of the flight.

Mattingly, who had been grounded, worked in a simulator with other engineers to find a way to start up the command module with very little power, because the normal procedure used more electricity than the batteries could spare. The new procedure was tested on the ground and then read to the crew. The crew made one further correction to the flight path on 14 April by hand, since the guidance platform in the lunar module had been shut down to save power. Lovell lined the spacecraft up using the Earth's terminator, the line between day and night, as a reference, and Haise timed a burn of about 14 seconds.

On 17 April, as the spacecraft approached Earth, the crew discarded the service module so that they could see the damage. Lovell reported that one whole panel was gone and that a large amount of equipment inside was visible and damaged. This was the first sight of the harm and it showed the ground that the heat shield on the command module was probably undamaged, since the blast had occurred on the opposite side. The crew then went back into Odyssey, powered up its systems in the order that had been worked out, and released the lunar module a short time before entry. Aquarius burned up in the atmosphere, and a small part of its radioactive fuel source fell into the Pacific, where it was not recovered.

Radio contact normally breaks during re-entry because of the ionised air around the capsule, and on Apollo missions the blackout lasted about three minutes. On this flight it ran longer, by roughly half a minute, which was the most anxious point on the ground. Odyssey then emerged from the blackout and the crew reported that they were safe. The three parachutes opened, and the capsule landed in the South Pacific on 17 April at 18:07 UTC, 142 hours and 54 minutes after launch. The helicopter carrier USS Iwo Jima picked the crew up within about 45 minutes. The astronauts were tired, thin and dehydrated, but they needed no urgent treatment, apart from Haise's infection.

A review board led by Edgar Cortright reported in June 1970 that the accident came from the combination of the damaged tank, the design change in the heater voltage that was not carried through the thermostats, and the test procedure. NASA changed the design of the oxygen tanks, removed the stirring fans, added a third tank, and put a battery in the service module as a reserve. Apollo 14 flew in January 1971 and landed at Fra Mauro. No crew was lost in the programme in flight, although three men had died in the Apollo 1 fire in 1967. Apollo 13 is remembered as a mission that did not reach the Moon, but whose crew and ground staff got three men home from a failure that nobody had planned for.
